James Watson and Francis Crick. The American biologist and British physicist who solved the three-dimensional structure of DNA in 1953, revealing the double helix and immediately suggesting the mechanism of hereditary replication that would found molecular biology.

Watson and Crick deduced the double helix structure of DNA from X-ray crystallography data, particularly from Photo 51 captured by Rosalind Franklin, combined with model-building. They published their discovery in Nature in 1953. Immediately, they recognised that the complementary base pairing, adenine with thymine and guanine with cytosine, implied a replication mechanism. Each strand serves as a template for a new partner strand, a mechanism so elegant that it almost explained itself.

Watson brought to their collaboration the traditions of the Phage Group in molecular biology, while Crick brought theoretical physics and deep structural reasoning. Their collaboration combined empiricism with abstraction in a way that proved extraordinarily powerful. Their model was elegant and correct on the first major attempt, an unusual achievement in science that marked both their insight and their good fortune.

Their work launched what Crick called the central dogma: DNA becomes RNA becomes Protein, the chain of information flow that became the foundation of molecular biology. Watson later established modern molecular genetics, while Crick pursued neuroscience and consciousness studies.

They shared the 1962 Nobel Prize with Maurice Wilkins, whose X-ray crystallography had provided crucial evidence. Rosalind Franklin, who had generated the critical images including Photo 51, had died and could not be nominated. Thomas Hunt Morgan had mapped genes before them, but Watson and Crick revealed the physical molecule genes were made from. Barbara McClintock's transposable elements were later explained at the molecular level through DNA structure, and the antibiotic resistance mechanisms that Fleming discovered would eventually be understood at the molecular level through these same insights into DNA.
